title: Can local learning match self-supervised backpropagation?
claim: Global backprop needs precise one-to-one error feedback; local rules with added top-down feedback better approximate it and close the performance gap.
layout: 5 panels: three network diagrams top, notation diagrams bottom-left, bar chart bottom-right
description: The top row has three neuron-graph diagrams that compare Backpropagation (A), local-SSL (B) and local-SSL with direct feedback (C). Blue circles are feedforward neurons, red circles are feedback or error neurons, and gray circles are inactive units. Green dashed or solid links mark gating signals. A green shaded oval highlights the layer containing the target synapse. A shared legend sits under the row. The bottom-left panel (D) shows stacked layer diagrams z^1 to z^L for global BP-SSL and local-SSL. Black arrows carry the weights W^l, and red arrows carry the transposed weights (W^l)^T or the projections B_*^l. The bottom-right panel (E) is a bar chart of STL-10 accuracy. A blue baseline bar reaches 73.29, and two orange bars reach 78.66 and 79.38. A green dashed line marks the BP-SSL level near 80. The eye goes first to the colorful network graphs.
caption: Overview of BP and local-SSL (A) To train the target synapse (blue), BP gradients need to be propagated down a one-to-one matching error network (red) that is gated (green) by the feedforward activations. (B): In Local-SSL, plasticity is modulated by predictive signals from same-layer lateral projections (red arrow) and global scalar values (green). (C) We show that local-SSL with feedback from the top layer better approximates BP. (D) Notations for theoretical analysis: In Section 3, we compare gradient updates of local-SSL and global BP-SSL. Both algorithms share the same feedforward weight W l and projection BL
abstract: While end-to-end self-supervised learning with backpropagation (global BP-SSL) has become central for training modern AI systems, theories of local self-supervised learning (local-SSL) have struggled to build functional representations in deep neural networks. To establish a link between global and local rules, we first develop a theory for deep linear networks: we identify conditions for local-SSL algorithms (like Forward-forward or CLAPP) to implement exactly the same weight update as a global BP-SSL. Starting from the theoretical insights, we then develop novel variants of local-SSL algorithms to approximate global BP-SSL in deep non-linear convolutional neural networks. Variants that improve the similarity between gradient updates of local-SSL with those of global BP-SSL also show better performance on image datasets (CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny ImageNet). The best local-SSL rule with the CLAPP loss function matches the performance of a comparable global BP-SSL with InfoNCE or CPC-like loss functions, and improves upon state-of-the-art for local SSL on these benchmarks.
